key_finding: Answer accuracy correlates more with cumulative retrieval recall than with number of searches or context consumed, and the best-performing agents issue far fewer redundant queries.
methodology: Trajectory-level diagnosis of six long-horizon search agents on BrowseComp-Plus and BrowseComp using human-annotated document-level relevance judgments to separate retrieval gaps from utilization gaps.
why_it_matters: Reframes what an 'agentic gain' should be measured against: not search effort or activity but cumulative retrieval recall and evidence utilization, which changes how our evaluation should attribute gains to specific mechanisms and when to stop searching.
limitations: Focused on general question-answering search agents rather than scholarly paper search specifically
Findings depend on the fixed retrieval model/harness used across the six agents evaluated
relevance_reason: Directly diagnoses where and why agentic search gains materialize or fail, the exact question the brief asks hardest for.

key_finding: PaSa-7B surpasses the best Google-based baseline by 37.78% in recall@20 and 39.90% in recall@50 on RealScholarQuery, and exceeds a prompted GPT-4o agent by 30.36% in recall.
methodology: RL-trained LLM agent that invokes search tools, reads papers, and selects references, trained on synthetic AutoScholarQuery (35k queries) and evaluated on a newly built real-world benchmark, RealScholarQuery.
why_it_matters: Establishes both the single-query search-engine baseline and a concrete, reproducible recall gain for an autonomous scholarly search agent, anchoring the recall-ceiling question the whole scan turns on.
limitations: Trained on synthetic queries though evaluated on a real benchmark
Gain attributed to the system as a whole rather than to individual agentic moves
relevance_reason: Foundational scholarly-search agent paper reporting quantified recall gains over single-query search-engine baselines with an explicit benchmark construction.

key_finding: A bounded pipeline of one seed search, 1.5-hop citation expansion, entailment-based pruning, and recency-aware random-walk ranking outperforms proprietary deep research agents by up to 3x recall@50 at roughly a third of the cost.
methodology: Structurally-bounded agentic graph exploration (Crase) evaluated on LitSearch and one further benchmark over a 500K-paper arXiv corpus.
why_it_matters: Isolates citation-graph traversal as the specific mechanism carrying the gain over open-ended deep-research loops, exactly the attribution the brief's second question asks for, and suggests a cheaper, more inspectable design.
limitations: Evaluated on a curated arXiv-only corpus of 500K papers, not the open web
Comparison baselines are proprietary deep research agents rather than a plain single-query search baseline
relevance_reason: Directly attributes a quantified retrieval gain to citation-graph traversal and pruning rather than to an undifferentiated agent system.

key_finding: Overlap between human- and AI-selected references across eight expert-conceived research projects was under 6%, and 64% of AI-generated references were real papers with at least one incorrect metadata field, though a single 2026-model test showed zero errors.
methodology: Controlled parallel literature-review study: human experts and mid-2025 LLMs (ChatGPT-4o, ChatGPT Deep Research, Gemini) perform identical review tasks on eight defined physics/astrophysics/cosmology projects, plus a single-project test of a 2026 model.
why_it_matters: Directly tests the premise that agentic/deep-research LLM literature review reproduces expert search; the low overlap and high metadata-error rate is exactly the kind of gain-failing-to-hold evidence the brief asks the scan to reach hardest for.
limitations: Domain-specific to physics/astrophysics/cosmology
Small sample of eight projects
2026-model result is a single-project anecdote, not a controlled comparison
relevance_reason: Empirically contradicts the premise that agentic LLM literature search matches expert-level recall, with a quantified overlap figure and hallucination/metadata-error rates.

key_finding: WisPaper achieves 22.26% recall on TaxoBench versus 20.92% for an O3 baseline, and its validation model attains 93.70% accuracy at rejecting hallucinated candidates.
methodology: abstract-only description of an integrated agent system (Scholar Search, Library, AI Feeds) evaluated on TaxoBench recall and validation accuracy.
why_it_matters: A modest, largely undifferentiated recall improvement over another agentic baseline (not a plain single-query search), offering little insight into which specific mechanism drives the gain or how the benchmark was built.
limitations: Gain over baseline is small (about 1.3 points) and the comparator is itself an agentic system, not a plain single-query baseline
No detail on TaxoBench construction or contamination controls
relevance_reason: An in-domain scholarly-search agent system report, but the gain is small and not mechanistically decomposed, so it is replaceable by stronger evidence already in this set.

key_finding: ReBOL, combining LLM query reformulation with Bayesian-optimization-guided document scoring, achieves 46.5% vs 35.0% recall@100 against the best LLM reranker on Robust04, with comparable latency.
methodology: Bayesian optimization over a multimodal relevance posterior initialized by LLM query reformulations, evaluated against LLM reranker baselines on five BEIR datasets with two LLMs.
why_it_matters: A concrete retrieval/reranking mechanism that decouples query reformulation from vector-similarity top-k limits, relevant as an underlying technique for future literature-search agents, though not tested in that setting.
limitations: Evaluated on general BEIR/Robust04 retrieval, not on a scientific-literature-search benchmark or an agentic system
No test of whether gains hold when embedded in an end-to-end search agent
relevance_reason: Offers a retrieval/reranking method combining query reformulation and Bayesian optimization, relevant to the brief's third scope item but demonstrated outside the scientific-literature-search setting.

key_finding: Removing followable hyperlinks between wiki pages roughly doubles the number of searches per grounded fact needed by a tool-using LLM agent at scale, though facts deemed 'unreachable by search' were recoverable via read-derived re-queries.
methodology: Pre-registered two-arm contrast on a deterministic generated wiki corpus at 50/500/5000 pages, comparing real cross-references versus meaning-preserving prose, measured across 99 episodes of a Claude agent.
why_it_matters: Suggests link/graph traversal reduces search cost at scale in a document-navigation setting, an analogue to citation-graph traversal in scholarly search, but demonstrated on an organizational wiki rather than scientific literature.
limitations: Corpus is a synthetic organizational wiki, not a scientific-literature corpus
Self-published/unclear peer review venue
No comparison to a database search recall ceiling
relevance_reason: Quantifies a link-traversal mechanism's effect on search cost, analogous to citation-graph traversal, but in a setting distinct from scientific literature search.

key_finding: LATTICE, an LLM-guided hierarchical search index with no embedding model at search time, achieves 46.7 nDCG@10 on BRIGHT matching the best fine-tuned ensemble, and 49.1 with a lightweight ensemble variant.
methodology: Top-down LLM-guided construction of a hierarchically navigable index over multi-level document summaries, with calibrated path-aggregated LLM traversal at query time; evaluated on BRIGHT plus NQ, SciFact, SciDocs.
why_it_matters: Demonstrates that embedding-based top-k retrieval is a real ceiling that reasoning-intensive queries can miss, and offers an LLM-guided traversal alternative relevant to the retrieval layer of literature-search agents, though evaluated mostly on general reasoning-intensive IR.
limitations: Primary benchmark (BRIGHT) spans general reasoning-intensive domains, not specifically scientific-literature search
Scientific IR results (SciFact, SciDocs) reported only as secondary competitiveness checks
relevance_reason: A retrieval/reranking method addressing the embedding-retriever recall ceiling directly, but its main evaluation setting is general reasoning-intensive retrieval rather than the brief's scientific-literature-search agents.

key_finding: On a fixed, human-verified corpus, BM25-paired Search-R1 reaches only 3.86% accuracy while GPT-5 reaches 55.9%, and pairing GPT-5 with a Qwen3-Embedding-8B retriever raises accuracy to 70.1% with fewer search calls.
methodology: Benchmark derived from BrowseComp with a fixed curated corpus, human-verified supporting documents and mined hard negatives, enabling controlled disentanglement of agent versus retriever contributions.
why_it_matters: Provides a controlled, reproducible baseline recall/accuracy ceiling for single-query retrieval (BM25) versus stronger retrievers and full agentic pipelines, the exact anchor the brief says every other reported gain must be measured against.
limitations: Corpus and negatives were mined per-query from the benchmark's own supporting documents, which later work shows can inflate retrieval-difficulty estimates
Web-QA style queries rather than scholarly literature search specifically
relevance_reason: The controlled benchmark underlying baseline-versus-agent comparisons that several other papers in this set build on or challenge.

key_finding: Context isolation at webpage-triage and final-answer-validation decision points (NIS-Agent) reduces token cost by 33% versus baseline while maintaining competitive performance across GAIA, WebWalkerQA, BrowseComp, and BrowseComp-zh.
methodology: Introduces the IBIS benchmark to measure 'inertia bias' (agents judging their own prior actions less objectively) and evaluates NIS-Agent's context-isolation fix across four deep-research benchmarks, plus an 8B model trained for intrinsic resistance.
why_it_matters: Identifies a specific, previously undiagnosed failure mode (self-authored action history biasing subsequent judgment) that degrades agentic search performance, and attributes a measured efficiency gain to a specific architectural fix rather than to the system as a whole.
limitations: Evaluated on general deep-research QA benchmarks rather than scholarly literature search specifically
IBIS benchmark is newly introduced and not yet independently validated
relevance_reason: Attributes a quantified gain to a specific agentic design fix (context isolation) and surfaces a failure mode relevant to interpreting other agents' reported gains.

key_finding: HySemRAG's structured field extraction achieves 35.1% higher semantic similarity than PDF-chunking approaches (0.655 vs 0.485, p<0.000001), with 99.0% citation accuracy in validated responses.
methodology: Hybrid semantic retrieval combining vector search, keyword filtering and knowledge-graph traversal with agentic self-correction, evaluated across 643 observations from 60 testing sessions and applied to geospatial epidemiology literature.
why_it_matters: A hybrid retrieval-plus-graph-traversal architecture for literature synthesis, relevant as an underlying method, but its evaluation targets extraction quality and citation accuracy rather than search recall, benchmark construction, or mechanism-specific attribution.
limitations: Applied case study is geospatial epidemiology, not a general literature-search benchmark
No comparison against a single-query search baseline or recall metric
relevance_reason: A hybrid retrieval/graph-traversal system for literature synthesis, touching the brief's retrieval-methods scope but not its core recall/benchmark/replication questions.

key_finding: A systematic taxonomy of Deep Research agents by information-acquisition strategy (API-based vs browser-based), tool-use framework, and planning architecture, with a critical evaluation identifying restricted external-knowledge access, sequential execution inefficiencies, and metric-objective misalignment in current benchmarks.
methodology: Narrative survey and taxonomy synthesis with a maintained repository of Deep Research agent research; abstract-only for specific findings.
why_it_matters: Gives the orientation the scan needs on how agentic literature/deep-research systems are built and evaluated, and explicitly names the benchmark-construction weaknesses the brief's third question asks the scan to surface.
limitations: Narrative rather than systematic review protocol
Abstract gives no quantitative findings
Not specific to scholarly/scientific literature search
relevance_reason: The synthesis and benchmark critique needed to compare across the individually-scoped papers in this set.

key_finding: Relocating BrowseComp-Plus's evidence into a 553M-document corpus built without reference to the benchmark drops the strongest agent's evidence recall from 84.3% to 21.4% and answer accuracy by five points while requiring 63% more search calls.
methodology: A dataset-agnostic projection pipeline decomposes questions into atomic reasoning hops and re-grounds each hop in ClimbMix, retaining only questions verified by automatic checks, an independent agent, and human review; applied to 830 BrowseComp-Plus questions to yield 57 fully grounded questions.
why_it_matters: Directly demonstrates that a benchmark's per-query-selected corpus inflates retrieval performance, and shows an agentic system's reported gain collapsing when the same questions are evaluated against a corpus not built around them -- the precise failure-to-replicate evidence the brief asks the scan to reach hardest for.
limitations: Yields only 57 fully grounded questions from 830, a small evaluation set
Single benchmark projection (BrowseComp-Plus to ClimbMix), not yet generalized to other benchmarks
relevance_reason: The clearest demonstration in this set that a reported agentic-search gain shrinks dramatically when the benchmark's corpus-construction advantage is removed.

key_finding: PaperPilot-9B improves multi-turn literature search over a base Qwen3.5-9B toolset agent, raising Hit@5 from 58.0 to 77.0, MRR from 47.5 to 59.4, and nDCG@10 from 26.8 to 32.5, while cutting workflow execution errors from 9.5% to 0%.
methodology: Trains a 9B agent via supervised workflow imitation and preference optimization over corrupted workflows; evaluates multi-turn interaction against a toolset-agent baseline using DAG-structured search operators (keyword search, citation expansion, filtering, scoring, reranking, evidence extraction).
why_it_matters: Directly demonstrates that explicit, editable workflows — including citation expansion and reranking as separable operators — carry the measured gain over an undifferentiated toolset agent, giving evidence for which specific agentic moves matter.
limitations: Baseline is a toolset agent, not a single-query database search baseline
benchmark construction details not given in the abstract
single model family (Qwen) tested
relevance_reason: A concrete, decomposed agentic literature-search system whose workflow structure lets specific moves (citation expansion, reranking) be inspected rather than treated as a black box.

key_finding: EviReform's evidence-guided query reformulation exceeds the strongest baseline by up to 5.59 Recall@5 points and 4.50 F1 points on 2WikiMultiHopQA, HotpotQA, and MuSiQue.
methodology: Introduces residual-query reformulation from retrieved passages, normalized and combined with the original retrieval signal and propagated across a proposition graph; evaluated on standard multi-hop QA benchmarks.
why_it_matters: Shows a specific reformulation mechanism, rather than the system as a whole, carrying a quantified retrieval gain — a template for isolating agentic-move contributions, though the setting is generic multi-hop QA rather than literature search.
limitations: Evaluated on general multi-hop QA benchmarks, not scientific literature search
no comparison to a single-query database search baseline
abstract gives no absolute recall numbers, only deltas
relevance_reason: Demonstrates isolating a reformulation mechanism's contribution to graph retrieval gain, relevant to the brief's second question even though the setting is off-domain.

key_finding: Screening 125 candidate autonomous-research-agent works and coding 26 in full, the survey finds 83% of runnable systems release code but only 38% release seeds/execution traces or report any novelty-verification method, and none of nine closed-loop L4 systems has an externally validated in-loop oracle.
methodology: Systematic survey with defined screening/inclusion criteria (125 screened, 35 included, 26 full-text coded) across seven audit dimensions covering the full AI-research lifecycle, including literature search.
why_it_matters: Establishes that claim-verification and reproducibility artifacts lag code release across agentic research systems, a caution directly relevant to how much weight to give reported agentic literature-search gains without independent verification.
limitations: Covers the full research lifecycle, not literature search specifically
abstract gives no numbers specific to search benchmarks
self-reported coding of included works
relevance_reason: Broad, systematically constructed survey of the verification gap across agentic research systems, directly bearing on how much weight to give unreplicated agentic-search claims.

key_finding: PaSaMaster achieves a 16.5x higher F1-score than Google Scholar and a 37.8% higher F1-score than GPT-5.2 at about 1% of the cost, reducing source hallucination from 32.66% to zero, across 38 disciplines in PaSaMaster-Bench.
methodology: Recursive self-evolving agentic retrieval system separating intent understanding (frontier LLM) from retrieval/scoring (lightweight models); evaluated against Google Scholar and GPT-5.2 on a purpose-built 38-discipline benchmark.
why_it_matters: Directly anchors the single-query database search baseline (Google Scholar) the brief needs, and quantifies how much a specific self-evolving retrieval mechanism adds on top, at a stated cost tradeoff.
limitations: Benchmark (PaSaMaster-Bench) is newly introduced by the same authors, with limited construction detail in the abstract
comparison partner (Google Scholar) is a product, not a controlled single-query retrieval baseline
no independent replication reported
relevance_reason: Gives an explicit, numeric single-query-search baseline comparison and attributes gain to a specific self-evolving retrieval mechanism — squarely answers the brief's first and second questions.

key_finding: PaperQA2 matches or exceeds subject-matter-expert performance on literature search, summarization, and contradiction-detection tasks, identifying 2.34±1.99 contradictions per paper with 70% validated by human experts.
methodology: Rigorous human-AI comparison methodology on real-world literature research tasks; introduces the LitQA2 benchmark used to guide system design; humans given full internet/tool access for a fair comparison.
why_it_matters: The landmark result the field measures itself against for whether agentic literature-search systems can exceed expert performance; any claim of superhuman synthesis should be compared to this specific benchmark and methodology.
limitations: Domain restricted to biology literature for the contradiction-detection task
no explicit single-query database search baseline reported in the abstract
results are from the system's own authors without independent replication mentioned
relevance_reason: The most cited, closest prior work in this exact space; its LitQA2 benchmark and human-comparison methodology are the reference point competing systems must be measured against.

key_finding: Across a custom agent harness and provider CLIs, grep-based retrieval generally yields higher accuracy than vector retrieval on a 116-question LongMemEval sample, but overall scores depend strongly on harness and tool-calling style.
methodology: Two empirical experiments comparing grep vs. vector retrieval across four agent harnesses, varying tool-output presentation and the amount of distracting surrounding context.
why_it_matters: Challenges the assumption that dense/vector retrieval is the right default retrieval mechanism for agentic search, and shows harness architecture confounds retrieval-method comparisons — a caution for how our benchmark comparisons should be designed.
limitations: Setting is conversational memory retrieval (LongMemEval), not scientific literature search
small sample (116 questions)
no citation-graph or literature-specific corpus tested
relevance_reason: A rare direct empirical test of a 'simple' baseline (grep/keyword) beating vector retrieval, relevant caution for baseline-ceiling claims, though tested off-domain.

key_finding: GraphRAG frequently underperforms vanilla RAG on many real-world tasks; GraphRAG-Bench systematically identifies the conditions under which graph structure does and does not provide measurable benefit.
methodology: Introduces a comprehensive benchmark spanning fact retrieval, complex reasoning, contextual summarization, and creative generation, with pipeline-wide evaluation from graph construction to generation.
why_it_matters: Directly interrogates whether graph-based retrieval — the mechanism underlying citation-graph traversal in agentic literature search — actually beats a simpler baseline, and under what conditions it fails, which is the kind of replication-failure evidence the brief asks us to weight most heavily.
limitations: Benchmark is general-purpose RAG, not built on scientific literature or citation graphs specifically
not evaluated on literature-search agents directly
relevance_reason: Empirically shows that graph retrieval, the analogue of citation-graph traversal, often fails to beat vanilla RAG — a direct challenge to a premise of agentic system design, though tested outside the literature-search setting.

key_finding: DynaKRAG ranks first among compared methods in EM and F1 across all nine dataset-backbone pairs on HotpotQA, 2Wiki, and MuSiQue, with 10.1-34.3% total-token efficiency gains and 15.1-43.4% retrieval-call efficiency gains.
methodology: Learns a shared state-conditioned policy coordinating iterative retrieval, query reformulation, evidence assessment, and sufficiency checking; evaluated with three backbones on three multi-hop QA benchmarks.
why_it_matters: Provides a template for attributing gains to specific evidence-control operations (reformulation, sufficiency-checking) rather than the agent as a whole, transferable in principle to literature-search agent design, though evaluated only on generic multi-hop QA.
limitations: Evaluated on generic multi-hop QA, not scientific literature retrieval
no single-query database search baseline reported
efficiency gains reported relative to a matched baseline rather than a database search ceiling
relevance_reason: A methodologically relevant example of decomposing agentic retrieval gains into discrete operations, useful analogy for the brief's second question despite an off-domain benchmark.

key_finding: Search-Time Contamination — where deep research agents retrieve benchmark metadata, question context, or ground-truth answers via web search — inflates measured performance by up to 4% across six public benchmarks.
methodology: Defines three contamination severity types (metadata leakage, question-context leakage, explicit answer leakage), develops detection algorithms, and applies them to evaluate modern deep research agents on six public benchmarks.
why_it_matters: Directly shows that reported gains for web-searching agents can be artifacts of benchmark contamination rather than genuine reasoning or retrieval improvement — exactly the kind of gain-replication-failure evidence the brief asks us to prioritize, and a warning to design contamination-aware evaluations for any agentic literature-search benchmark we build.
limitations: Focused on deep research/web agents generally rather than literature-search agents specifically
measured inflation (up to 4%) may understate contamination in less controlled benchmarks
detection algorithms rely on identifiable leakage patterns that may miss subtler contamination
relevance_reason: The clearest evidence in the batch that reported agentic gains can fail to hold once benchmark contamination is accounted for — directly answers the brief's fourth and most-emphasized question.

key_finding: Deep Research Bench's frozen-web 'RetroSearch' environment yields agent performance comparable to live-web evaluation across 89 multi-step research tasks, enabling reliable, reproducible benchmarking of web research agents over time.
methodology: Introduces 89 multi-step web-research tasks across 8 categories with human-worked answers, a frozen scraped-web snapshot for reproducible evaluation, and automated trace analysis of hallucination, tool use, and forgetting.
why_it_matters: Supplies a concrete, reusable benchmark-construction methodology (task sourcing, answer curation, contamination control via a frozen web snapshot) directly relevant to the brief's third question of how literature-search-agent evaluation sets should be built.
limitations: Tasks are general web research, not scientific literature search specifically
89 task instances is a modest sample
frozen snapshot may not capture literature-specific corpora like citation databases
relevance_reason: A rigorous, reproducibility-focused benchmark-construction template (query sourcing, human-labeled answers, contamination control) that any literature-search benchmark should be compared against.

key_finding: State-of-the-art retrieval models perform far worse on reasoning-intensive queries than on standard benchmarks — the leading MTEB model scores 59.0 nDCG@10 generally but only 18.3 on BRIGHT — though explicit query reasoning recovers up to 12.2 points.
methodology: Introduces 1,384 real-world, reasoning-intensive queries across diverse domains (economics, psychology, math, coding), curated from naturally occurring human data, and evaluates state-of-the-art embedding/retrieval models.
why_it_matters: Establishes a concrete, widely-cited ceiling for single-query embedding search on reasoning-intensive retrieval (18.3 nDCG@10 vs. 59.0 on standard tasks) — precisely the recall-ceiling anchor the brief's first question needs, and shows reformulation-style reasoning partially recovers the gap.
limitations: Domains are general (coding, math, economics), not scientific literature search specifically
no citation-graph or iterative-crawling agent evaluated
gap may differ for literature-specific corpora
relevance_reason: The most concrete, quantified baseline-ceiling result for single-query retrieval on hard queries in the batch, widely used as a reference in the agentic search literature this scan surveys.

key_finding: Agents-K1 converts raw scientific documents into agent-native knowledge graphs (entities, evidence, citations, typed relations) across 2.46 million papers, producing the Scholar-KG resource, and reports superior performance in scientific information extraction, KG construction, and multi-hop scientific reasoning.
methodology: Combines a five-module multimodal parser, a 4B information-extraction backbone trained with GRPO, and a tri-source agent CLI unifying web search, multimodal graph retrieval, and cross-document traversal; applied at scale to 2.46M papers.
why_it_matters: Directly instantiates citation-graph traversal beyond flat citation edges (typed relations, claims, evidence, method lineages) at a scale relevant to designing a production-grade literature-search agent's graph layer.
limitations: Abstract gives no quantitative benchmark numbers or comparison to a single-query baseline
benchmark/evaluation construction not detailed
superiority claims stated without effect sizes
relevance_reason: A concrete demonstration of richer, typed citation-graph representations for literature-search agents, directly informing the brief's question about what graph traversal adds beyond flat citation edges.

key_finding: An instruction-tuned agent with DPO that dynamically chooses between GraphRAG and VectorRAG achieves a 0.63 gain in Vector-Store Context Recall and a 0.56 gain in overall Context Precision over baseline on synthetic benchmarks mimicking real-world literature-review queries.
methodology: Agentic pipeline ingesting PubMed/arXiv/Google Scholar data into a Neo4j citation knowledge graph and a FAISS vector store, with an LLM agent choosing GraphRAG vs. VectorRAG per query and quantifying uncertainty; evaluated with bootstrapped metrics on synthetic benchmarks.
why_it_matters: A worked example of dynamic graph/vector routing for scientific literature review, but evaluated only on synthetic queries mimicking real ones, which limits how much its reported gains can be trusted without an independently-labeled benchmark.
limitations: Evaluation is on synthetic benchmarks, not independently constructed or human-labeled queries
no comparison to a single-query database search baseline
dynamic-routing gain not isolated from other pipeline changes
relevance_reason: Directly in the brief's setting (scientific literature review, hybrid graph/vector retrieval) but its synthetic-benchmark evaluation is exactly the kind of weak construction the brief asks us to be skeptical of.

key_finding: Sparse (keyword-based) retrieval achieves results close to state-of-the-art dense retrieval for scientific literature search/distillation, and the system increases coverage of relevant documents for literature-review generation.
methodology: LLM-based agentic system for literature search and distillation, evaluated on biology-related QA drawn from prior literature benchmarks; compares sparse vs dense retrieval. Abstract-only for specific numbers.
why_it_matters: Suggests the simple sparse-retrieval baseline sits closer to the recall ceiling than assumed, weakening the case that dense retrieval or added agentic complexity is needed — directly bears on the baseline-ceiling question.
limitations: Domain restricted to biology QA benchmarks
No explicit precision/recall numbers reported in the abstract
Unclear generalization to other scientific domains
relevance_reason: Directly tests whether simple sparse retrieval matches more complex approaches for scientific literature review, informing the baseline-ceiling question.

key_finding: Search-based LLM agents surface benchmark answers directly on retrieved sources (e.g., HuggingFace) for ~3% of queries across HLE, SimpleQA and GPQA; blocking that source drops accuracy by ~15% on the contaminated subset.
methodology: Empirical audit of search-agent reasoning logs across three capability benchmarks, plus an ablation experiment blocking a contamination source. Abstract-only for further detail.
why_it_matters: Demonstrates that measured gains from search-based agents can be substantially inflated by search-time contamination, meaning reported agentic improvements over baselines may not reflect genuine capability — a direct answer to where reported gains fail to hold up.
limitations: Benchmarks tested are general capability sets, not literature-search-specific
Contamination source characterized mainly via HuggingFace; other sources acknowledged but not fully mapped
relevance_reason: Provides direct evidence that reported agentic-search gains can evaporate once benchmark contamination is controlled for — exactly the failure mode the brief asks us to check for.

key_finding: CG-RAG's citation-graph-aware hybrid sparse+dense retrieval (LeSeGR) significantly outperforms RAG baselines combined with various state-of-the-art retrieval methods on multi-domain research question-answering benchmarks.
methodology: Contextual graph representation of citation graphs integrated with lexical-semantic hybrid retrieval and graph-aware generation; evaluated across multiple domain research-QA benchmarks. Abstract-only for effect sizes.
why_it_matters: Isolates citation-graph traversal plus hybrid retrieval as the specific mechanisms driving gains over plain RAG, directly addressing which agentic move carries the improvement.
limitations: Abstract omits quantitative effect sizes
Not explicitly benchmarked against a pure single-query recall ceiling
relevance_reason: Directly evaluates citation-graph traversal as a distinct mechanism for literature-search-style retrieval, the exact concern of the agentic-mechanism question.

key_finding: On FRAMES, state-of-the-art LLMs achieve only 0.40 accuracy on multi-hop questions with no retrieval, rising to 0.66 (>50% improvement) with a proposed multi-step retrieval pipeline.
methodology: New unified RAG evaluation dataset (FRAMES) of multi-hop questions; baseline no-retrieval vs multi-step retrieval pipeline comparison. Abstract-only for further detail.
why_it_matters: Quantifies a large baseline-to-retrieval-pipeline gap, a useful reference point for the recall-ceiling question, but the setting is general open-domain QA rather than scientific literature search.
limitations: General QA domain, not scientific literature search specifically
Abstract does not specify the mechanics of 'multi-step retrieval'
relevance_reason: Offers a clean single-query vs multi-step retrieval baseline comparison analogous to the recall-ceiling question, in a different domain.

key_finding: Mind2Web 2's Agent-as-a-Judge framework evaluates ten frontier agentic search systems on 130 long-horizon tasks; the best system (OpenAI Deep Research) reaches only 50-70% of human performance despite spending half the time.
methodology: New benchmark of 130 realistic long-horizon web-browsing tasks built with over 1000 human-labor hours; tree-structured-rubric judge agents assess correctness and source attribution.
why_it_matters: Provides a rigorous benchmark-construction template (tree-rubric agent-as-judge evaluation) for long-horizon agentic search that could be adapted for literature-search agents, though the task domain here is general web research rather than scientific literature.
limitations: Domain is general web browsing/deep research, not scientific literature specifically
Evaluation relies on LLM judges rather than gold document sets
relevance_reason: A closely related benchmark-construction precedent for evaluating long-horizon agentic search, adjacent to but not within the literature-search setting.

key_finding: ReMindRAG's LLM-guided graph traversal with edge-embedding memory replay outperforms existing KG-RAG baselines across benchmark datasets and LLM backbones while reducing token and inference costs.
methodology: Train-free memory mechanism embedded in knowledge-graph edges guiding node exploration/exploitation; evaluated across multiple KG-RAG benchmarks. Abstract-only for numeric results.
why_it_matters: Demonstrates memory-guided graph traversal as a cost-efficient mechanism for retrieval gains, conceptually relevant to citation-graph traversal, though evaluated on generic knowledge graphs rather than paper citation graphs.
limitations: Generic knowledge graphs, not citation graphs of scientific literature
No numeric results given in the abstract
relevance_reason: Illustrates a graph-traversal gain mechanism conceptually transferable to citation-graph-based literature search, tested outside the literature-search setting.

key_finding: A three-agent (Query, Retrieval, Learning) hybrid BM25+FAISS literature search system achieves 8.5% higher precision, 7.3% higher recall, and ~210ms lower latency than PaperQA and Semantic Scholar.
methodology: FastAPI-based multi-agent architecture with hybrid sparse/dense retrieval and Sentence-Transformer semantic matching; experimental comparison against published systems. Abstract-only for further detail.
why_it_matters: Directly quantifies an agentic system's gain over established literature-search baselines, giving a concrete effect-size data point for the agentic-vs-baseline question, though the unpublished, low-citation status limits confidence.
limitations: No peer-reviewed venue and only 1 citation, limiting confidence
Abstract does not decompose which agent drives the improvement
No description of evaluation dataset construction
relevance_reason: Directly on-topic (agentic scientific literature search vs baselines) with quantified gains, but quality/rigor concerns place it below stronger evidence.

key_finding: InfoDeepSeek introduces a benchmark of challenging, dynamic-web queries built to satisfy determinacy, difficulty, and diversity criteria, showing existing static, fixed-corpus benchmarks fail to elicit genuine agentic information-seeking behavior.
methodology: New benchmark-construction methodology plus a fine-grained evaluation framework (accuracy, utility, compactness); extensive experiments across LLMs and search engines. Abstract-only for numeric results.
why_it_matters: Provides a template for constructing literature-search-agent benchmarks that avoids the static, easily-gamed corpora that inflate reported gains, directly informing the benchmark-construction question, though tested on general web information-seeking.
limitations: General web information-seeking domain, not scientific literature specifically
Abstract lacks quantitative headline results
relevance_reason: Offers a rigorous benchmark-construction methodology addressing exactly the pitfalls the brief worries about, in a closely related but not identical setting.

key_finding: OpenNovelty, an agentic system for scholarly novelty assessment, retrieves and hierarchically organizes prior work to generate evidence-grounded novelty reports, deployed on 500+ ICLR 2026 submissions.
methodology: Four-phase pipeline (claim extraction, semantic-search retrieval, taxonomy construction, full-text comparison); deployed system with preliminary qualitative analysis, no formal benchmark metrics.
why_it_matters: Shows a real-world deployed agentic literature-retrieval pipeline for a downstream task (novelty assessment) adjacent to, but distinct from, direct literature search evaluation.
limitations: No quantitative recall/precision or benchmark evaluation reported
Task is novelty assessment rather than literature search itself
Preliminary/qualitative analysis only
relevance_reason: Demonstrates an agentic retrieval pipeline applied to scientific literature, but without benchmark evidence bearing on the brief's recall/gain questions.

key_finding: A systematic survey categorizes the deep-research agent pipeline into planning, question developing, web exploration, and report generation stages, summarizing optimization techniques and benchmarks for each.
methodology: Narrative/systematic literature survey of autonomous research agents; abstract-only, no primary experiments.
why_it_matters: Provides the field-wide map of techniques and benchmarks that lets us locate individual system and benchmark papers against the whole agentic-search pipeline, and flags open gaps to watch.
limitations: Survey/abstract-only, no independent empirical validation
Not exclusively scoped to scientific literature search agents (broader 'deep research')
relevance_reason: The synthesis needed to place individual system and benchmark papers within the overall agentic-search pipeline the brief is scanning.

key_finding: ReasonIR-8B, trained via a synthetic hard-query/hard-negative generation pipeline, achieves 29.9 nDCG@10 (36.9 with reranker) on the BRIGHT reasoning-IR benchmark and improves RAG performance on MMLU (+6.4%) and GPQA (+22.6%) over closed-book baselines.
methodology: Synthetic training-data generation producing reasoning-intensive queries and hard negatives per document; retriever trained and evaluated on BRIGHT and downstream RAG tasks. Abstract-only for further detail.
why_it_matters: A state-of-the-art reasoning-aware retriever is exactly the kind of underlying retrieval technique that could raise the recall ceiling for literature-search agents handling complex, multi-hop scientific queries, though evaluated on general reasoning benchmarks rather than scientific literature retrieval.
limitations: Evaluated on general reasoning-IR benchmarks (BRIGHT, MMLU, GPQA), not scientific-literature-specific corpora
Not tested on literature-search benchmarks directly
relevance_reason: A leading retrieval-method advance directly relevant to the retrieval/reranking sub-criterion, tested outside the literature-search setting.

key_finding: OpenScholar, a retrieval-augmented LM over 45M open-access papers, outperforms GPT-4o by 5% and PaperQA2 by 7% in correctness on the new ScholarQABench benchmark (2,967 expert queries), while GPT-4o hallucinates citations 78-90% of the time versus OpenScholar's expert-level citation accuracy.
methodology: Specialized retriever plus open datastore and self-feedback inference loop; evaluated on a newly constructed multi-domain benchmark (ScholarQABench) plus human expert preference studies.
why_it_matters: A flagship literature-synthesis system with its own purpose-built multi-domain benchmark and human-expert comparison gives the strongest concrete anchor for both the baseline-comparison and benchmark-construction questions in the brief's exact setting.
limitations: Benchmark and datastore are the authors' own construction, raising potential evaluation bias
Coverage limited to open-access papers only
relevance_reason: The most directly on-topic system-plus-benchmark pairing for agentic scientific literature synthesis, anchoring both baseline and benchmark-construction evidence.

key_finding: LitSearch, a 597-query literature-search retrieval benchmark, finds a 24.8-point recall@5 gap between BM25 and state-of-the-art dense retrievers, with LLM-based reranking adding a further 4.4% improvement, while commercial search engines like Google lag 32 points behind the best dense retriever.
methodology: Benchmark of 597 realistic literature-search queries built from GPT-4-generated questions on cited paragraphs plus author-written questions about recent papers, expert-reviewed; extensive retrieval and LLM-reranking comparisons.
why_it_matters: Directly establishes the quantitative baseline recall ceiling (BM25 vs dense) and demonstrates a benchmark-construction methodology (GPT-4-generated plus author-written queries) — the single most load-bearing anchor for both the recall-ceiling and benchmark-construction questions in the brief.
limitations: Scoped to ML/NLP papers only, not broader scientific domains
No agentic/iterative-crawling system evaluated, only static retrieval and reranking
relevance_reason: The clearest, most quantified answer to the brief's first and third questions (baseline recall ceiling and benchmark construction) within the exact literature-search setting.

key_finding: Introduces DeepResearch Bench, 100 PhD-level research tasks across 22 fields, with two novel evaluation methodologies — a reference-based report-quality assessment and a citation-accuracy/effective-citation-count framework for evaluating deep research agents' retrieval and collection capabilities.
methodology: Benchmark construction paper: expert-crafted task set plus two proposed evaluation frameworks validated for alignment with human judgment; open-sourced. Abstract-only for validation numbers.
why_it_matters: Gives a concrete, expert-vetted precedent for how literature/research-agent benchmarks are being constructed (task sourcing, reference-based scoring, citation-accuracy metrics) — directly informs how our own benchmark-construction criterion should be evaluated and what construction choices to scrutinize in other systems' reported gains.
limitations: targets general 'deep research agents' producing analyst reports rather than agents specifically doing scientific literature retrieval
no comparison against a single-query database search baseline
does not attribute gains to specific agentic mechanisms (reformulation, graph traversal, iterative crawling)
abstract gives no quantitative alignment or performance figures
relevance_reason: Directly addresses benchmark-construction (C4) for agentic research/literature agents, including a citation-accuracy evaluation framework relevant to retrieval assessment.
